summary: Brick tower on an iron caisson at the mouth of New Bedford Harbor, lit in 1898, automated in 1978 and off federal service since 2014.

lens.where: original fifth-order Fresnel; current optic is an RB-300 rotating unit

structures.note: Cast-iron caisson foundation with a brick tower; 53 ft (16.2 m) to the lantern per USLHS

access.note: Privately owned by a non-profit; reached only by boat; tower closed to visitors.

facts.agency: Mass Light (non-profit), owner since the 2015 auction

events.note: Keeper towed a disabled motor boat with three men to a wharf, 8 May 1914
Keeper rescued three men whose boat capsized near the light, April 1919
Keeper commended for assistance to the disabled sloop Empress, May 1921
Keeper towed a man in a rowboat who had lost an oar, February 1923
Keeper alone at the light during the 1938 New England hurricane (LighthouseFriends)
Coast Guard keepers took over operation after Charles A. Baker retired
Coast Guard announced plans to deactivate the light and move the beacon to the hurricane barrier
Revocable license to the City of New Bedford to operate the light as a private aid
Discontinued as an aid to navigation (LighthouseFriends, New England Lighthouses); USLHS still lists it as active
Sold at auction; high bid $80,000 on 23 November 2015

corrections.proposed: discontinued as a federal aid to navigation (2014); private aid status unconfirmed
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends and New England Lighthouses both say the light was discontinued as an aid to navigation in 2014; USLHS still lists it as active and Cyberlights says it is operational. Needs a Coast Guard Light List check before editing.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination prints the name 'F. Hopkinton Smith'; LighthouseFriends, New England Lighthouses and Cyberlights give F. Hopkinson Smith (Francis Hopkinson Smith, 1838-1915). The story uses the fuller name and notes the spelling.

The Board appropriated $45,000 (1895). LighthouseFriends reports the contract bid at $33,800; New England Lighthouses gives the cost as $34,000. These are different figures for different things (appropriation, bid, final cost).
LighthouseFriends dates the white paint to 1899. The Board's report for the year ended 30 June 1899 records 'Color of tower changed November 8, 1898'.

resolved_conflicts.field: fog signal move to hurricane barrier
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination places the fog signal move in the 1978 automation; New England Lighthouses dates a new automatic light and fog signal on the barrier to 1975, and Cyberlights reports the 1975 announcement.

notes_for_editor: Roster: 57 lines from the USLHS place record (archive's own roles; 'USCG' lines normalised to other). Not every line was checked against a primary record; the Baker, Hindley and Chase lines match the Board and Bulletin mentions. Pages: the Board volumes have OCR page indexes only for some pages; scan pages 325 (1894), 90 (1899) are image numbers, printed pages not read. The NRHP OCR reads 'F. Hopkinton Smith'; check the page image before publishing the spelling. Wikipedia gives 'F. Abraham Smith' and is not used. The light's current status is unresolved: USLHS says active, Cyberlights says operational, LighthouseFriends and New England Lighthouses say not an active aid since 2014. The NRHP listing date (1987-06-15) and the characteristic (Fl G 2.5s, from the record) were not verified from a source we read. LighthouseFriends material (Captain Baker's logs, the 1938 account, the 1962 drownings) is second-hand; the names of the 1962 casualties and of the 1998-2019 volunteers and Mass Light directors were left out as private individuals. The brief dates this batch 2026-10-22; the system date was 2026-10-27, which is the accessed date used. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the sentence 'by the end of this year' is in the Board's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1897 (scan page 301, after the FY1897 heading at scan page 253), not the 1896 report as first drafted; the story now says so. The NRHP printed text reads 'F. Hopkinton Smith' (checked on the page image, form p. 2). The fog bell is the Board's 'Shipman engine' (1899 report); LighthouseFriends' 'steam engine' is not used. Story footnotes now give scan pages for the 1895, 1897 and 1899 reports and the NRHP form page (p. 2).
